items.explanation: The cartoon shows a missionary peering through a telescope at distant lands while ragged, suffering poor crowd unnoticed at his feet — a critique of churches spending energy on foreign converts while ignoring poverty in American cities.
options: (A) Missionaries fixated on overseas converts while ignoring poverty at home.
(B) Open immigration was destabilizing the American economy.
(C) The United States should embrace overseas imperialism.
(D) The widening gap between rich and poor was creating a revolutionary situation.
items.stem: [Image description: Victor Gillam, 'Overlooked — or The Folly of Foreign Missions,' Judge magazine, 1895. A Protestant missionary peers through a telescope toward distant lands, oblivious to impoverished, suffering figures huddled at his feet.] The cartoonist's point of view is which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Correct. Gillam's 1895 cartoon shows a Protestant missionary peering through a telescope toward distant lands, oblivious to the ragged, suffering poor huddled at his feet. The title says it plainly: 'The Folly of Foreign Missions.' The cartoonist's point is one of misplaced priorities — churches spending money and energy converting people overseas while ignoring the poverty, sweatshops, and slums of American cities right in front of them.
option_explanations.B: Immigration is not the cartoon's subject. The figures at the missionary's feet represent the urban poor generally, and the critique is aimed at the churches' priorities — foreign missions versus domestic poverty — not at whether immigration was destabilizing the economy.
option_explanations.C: The cartoon argues against overseas ventures, not for them. Its whole point is that American churches should turn their attention homeward instead of gazing abroad; embracing overseas imperialism would be the telescope's direction, which the cartoonist calls folly.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon warns about neglected poverty, not about revolution. Nothing in the image suggests the poor are about to rise up; the critique is moral — the churches' indifference — not a prediction of class revolution.

items.explanation: Settlement houses (Hull House, 1889, and 400+ more by the 1910s) existed precisely to serve the urban poor the cartoon says missionaries ignored — direct aid to immigrants and working-class families in American cities.
options: (A) The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.
(B) The Spanish-American War of 1898.
(C) The Supreme Court's Insular Cases decisions on overseas territories.
(D) The settlement-house movement serving the urban poor.
items.stem: A reader sympathetic to the cartoon would most likely also have supported which of the following?

option_explanations.A: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred Chinese laborers from immigrating — a nativist, exclusionary measure. Someone sympathetic to a cartoon pleading for the urban poor would not support slamming the door on immigrants; exclusion is the opposite impulse from the cartoon's compassion.
option_explanations.B: The Spanish-American War (1898) was the overseas imperialism the cartoon criticizes — the telescope pointed outward. A reader who agreed that foreign ventures distracted from poverty at home would oppose, not support, a war of overseas expansion.
option_explanations.C: The Insular Cases (1901) upheld American colonial rule over overseas territories like Puerto Rico and the Philippines — the legal architecture of empire. That is the foreign-missions direction the cartoon calls folly, not the domestic charity it demands.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Settlement houses — Hull House (1889) and more than 400 others by the 1910s — existed to serve exactly the people at the missionary's feet: the urban poor, immigrants, and working-class families of American cities. A reader moved by the cartoon's plea to help poverty at home would naturally support the movement doing that work.

items.explanation: The cartoon shows exhausted women and children filing into a cannery, driven by a male figure labeled 'New York State Legislature' whose whip ends in the words '72 hours a week' — the suffragist argument that only the ballot would let women force legislatures to end child labor and sweatshop hours.
options: (A) Women deserved the vote because their economic contributions equaled men's.
(B) Women should not vote because they were too timid for rough male politics.
(C) Women needed the vote because male legislatures would not protect child workers.
(D) Women should not vote because their home and work duties left them no time for politics.
items.stem: [Image description: Rollin Kirby, 'Until Women Vote,' Woman's Journal, 1915. Weary women and dejected children enter a cannery, prodded by a male figure labeled 'New York State Legislature'; the lash of his whip reads '72 hours a week.'] The cartoon's main argument is which of the following?

option_explanations.A: The cartoon's argument is not about women's economic contributions matching men's. Its logic is protective and political: women and children are being crushed by 72-hour weeks in canneries, male legislatures will not stop it, so women need the ballot as a weapon to force reform. Economic equality is not the claim being made.
option_explanations.B: This is an anti-suffrage argument, and the cartoon is a suffragist weapon. Published in the Woman's Journal, it demands the vote for women; it does not argue women are too timid for politics.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Kirby's 1915 cartoon shows weary women and dejected children filing into a cannery, prodded by a male figure labeled 'New York State Legislature' whose whip ends in the words '72 hours a week.' The argument: male legislatures permit the exploitation of women and child workers, so women need the vote to compel the protective legislation men will not pass on their own — suffrage as the instrument of workplace reform.
option_explanations.D: Another anti-suffrage argument, opposite to the cartoon's message. The cartoon insists women must vote precisely because their work and family lives are at stake — it treats politics as necessary to protect women, not as something they have no time for.

items.explanation: Progressives backed both planks of the cartoon — women's suffrage and workplace reform (child-labor laws, hours limits, factory inspection) — as part of their broad program against Gilded Age laissez-faire.
options: (A) Members of the New York State legislature depicted in the cartoon.
(B) Defenders of the 'cult of domesticity.'
(C) Members of the Progressive reform movement.
(D) Adherents of Social Darwinism.
items.stem: Which group would have been most likely to endorse the cartoon's perspective?

option_explanations.A: The legislature is the cartoon's villain — the male figure literally driving women and children into the cannery with a whip labeled '72 hours a week.' Its members would hardly endorse a cartoon depicting them as exploiters.
option_explanations.B: Defenders of the 'cult of domesticity' believed women's proper sphere was the home, not politics or the factory — they opposed women's suffrage and public activism. The cartoon demands the ballot for women and attacks the conditions of women's wage labor, both of which domesticity's defenders rejected.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Progressives backed both of the cartoon's planks: women's suffrage and workplace reform — child-labor laws, hours limits, factory inspection. The cartoon is a Progressive argument in visual form: use democratic power (the vote) to curb the abuses of Gilded Age laissez-faire.
option_explanations.D: Social Darwinists opposed both halves of the cartoon's program: they regarded government intervention in the economy as interference with natural selection and generally opposed expanding the suffrage. The cartoon's demand for protective legislation is exactly what Social Darwinism condemned.

items.explanation: The cartoon demands government action against child labor and exploitative hours — the Progressive-era version of the enduring debate over how far federal, state, and local governments should intervene in the economy, recurring in the New Deal, the Great Society, and beyond.
options: (A) Ongoing debates over the proper role of government in regulating the economy.
(B) Ongoing debates over the proper role of political parties.
(C) Ongoing debates over states' power to defy federal authority.
(D) Ongoing debates over whether communities may outlaw behavior they deem immoral.
items.stem: The cartoon's ideas most directly reflect which continuity in American history?

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon demands that government act — through suffrage-won legislation — against child labor and exploitative hours. That is the Progressive-era form of the enduring American debate over how far government should intervene in the economy: the same argument recurs in the New Deal's labor standards, the Great Society's programs, and every later fight over regulation.
option_explanations.B: The cartoon is not about political parties or their proper role. No party appears in the image or the argument; the issue is government power over the economy, not party organization.
option_explanations.C: States defying federal authority — nullification, interposition — is a different debate entirely. The cartoon asks legislatures to act, not to resist Washington; federal-state conflict is nowhere in its argument.
option_explanations.D: Outlawing behavior deemed immoral — prohibition, gambling bans — is the moral-reform debate, not this one. The cartoon is about economic regulation (hours, child labor), not about criminalizing vice.

items.explanation: Cohen traces how Chicago's industrial workers moved from private welfare capitalism and anti-unionism to embracing the federal welfare state and industrial unionism. Those workers became the core of the New Deal Democratic coalition — urban, ethnic, labor-based — that dominated national politics for a generation.
options: (A) A sharp decline in voter turnout during the 1930s.
(B) The rise of a Republican majority in the Sunbelt states.
(C) The passage of the Taft-Hartley Act.
(D) The emergence of a durable Democratic majority anchored by urban industrial workers.
items.stem: Cohen's account best helps explain which of the following political developments?
items.stimulus: How industrial workers in one American city lived through an era when the nation shifted from relying on private welfare capitalism to building a welfare state — and from fighting the organization of its industrial workforce to accepting it. — paraphrased from Lizabeth Cohen, Making a New Deal: Industrial Workers in Chicago, 1919–1939 (1990)

option_explanations.A: Voter turnout rose, not fell, in the 1930s — the Depression politicized millions, and 1940 saw one of the highest turnouts of the century. Cohen's account of workers embracing the Democratic coalition describes mobilization, not withdrawal.
option_explanations.B: The Sunbelt Republican majority is a post-1960s development — suburbanization, the civil-rights realignment, and the Reagan coalition — decades after and largely separate from Cohen's 1919–1939 Chicago workers. Her account explains the New Deal coalition's construction, not its later Sunbelt unraveling.
option_explanations.C: The Taft-Hartley Act (1947) restricted unions — it was the backlash against the labor power Cohen describes, not the political development her account explains. Her narrative ends with workers accepting industrial unionism; Taft-Hartley was the counterattack on that achievement.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Cohen traces how Chicago's industrial workers moved from reliance on private welfare capitalism (company benefits, ethnic mutual aid) to the federal welfare state, and from resisting industrial unions to embracing them. Those workers — urban, ethnic, labor-based — became the core of the New Deal Democratic coalition that dominated national politics for a generation.

items.explanation: The New Deal's strongest institutional opponents were conservative justices who struck down the NIRA (Schechter, 1935) and the AAA (Butler, 1936) — prompting FDR's 1937 court-packing plan — joined by conservatives in Congress.
options: (A) Communist Party radicals and other political radicals.
(B) Organizations lobbying for senior citizens.
(C) Civil-rights groups such as the Congress of Racial Equality.
(D) Conservatives in Congress and on the Supreme Court.
items.stem: Which of the following most strongly tried to block or undo the changes Cohen describes?

option_explanations.A: Communist Party radicals supported the changes Cohen describes — they organized industrial workers and backed the welfare state, often pushing the New Deal from the left. They were allies of the transformation in its early years, not its blockers.
option_explanations.B: Organizations lobbying for senior citizens — like the Townsend clubs demanding old-age pensions — pushed for more welfare-state action, not less. They were part of the pressure for Social Security, not opponents of the New Deal's direction.
option_explanations.C: The Congress of Racial Equality was a civil-rights organization fighting segregation; it had no quarrel with the welfare state or industrial unionism. It was not an institutional opponent of the New Deal order.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The New Deal's most powerful institutional opponents were conservatives in Congress and on the Supreme Court: the justices struck down the NIRA in Schechter (1935) and the AAA in Butler (1936), and the resulting confrontation produced FDR's 1937 court-packing plan. Congressional conservatives joined the Court in trying to block or roll back the new federal role.

items.explanation: LBJ's Great Society — the Civil Rights Acts, the War on Poverty, Medicare/Medicaid — extended the New Deal's premise of federal responsibility for welfare and economic security into the 1960s.
options: (A) Senator Joseph McCarthy's anti-Communist crusade and loyalty investigations of the 1950s.
(B) President Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs of the 1960s.
(C) President Ronald Reagan's domestic agenda of the 1980s.
(D) The 1990s 'Contract with America.'
items.stem: The changes Cohen describes were later reinforced by which of the following?

option_explanations.A: McCarthy's anti-Communist crusade attacked the left and purged suspected subversives from government and unions — it weakened the labor-left coalition and chilled reform, rather than reinforcing the welfare state and union acceptance Cohen describes.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Lyndon Johnson's Great Society — the Civil Rights Acts, the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid — extended the New Deal's premise into the 1960s: that the federal government bears responsibility for citizens' welfare and economic security. It was the second great wave of the transformation Cohen traces.
option_explanations.C: Reagan's domestic agenda moved in the opposite direction: cutting domestic programs, deregulating, and declaring that government was the problem. It was an assault on the New Deal order, not a reinforcement of it.
option_explanations.D: The 1994 'Contract with America' sought to shrink the federal government — welfare reform, balanced budgets, devolution. Like Reaganism, it aimed to roll back the welfare-state premises Cohen describes, not reinforce them.

items.explanation: Black's majority opinion insisted the exclusion rested 'not on racial hostility but on wartime military judgments about invasion fears and security,' expressly rejecting the claim — pressed by Korematsu and the dissenters — that the policy was racial prejudice dressed up as military necessity. The opinion accepted congressional authorization, took invasion fears as sincere, and deferred to the military on all other points.
options: (A) That Congress had given the military legal authority to issue the exclusion orders.
(B) That fears of a West Coast invasion were sincerely held by military commanders.
(C) That the exclusion order was driven by racial prejudice rather than genuine military necessity.
(D) That courts should defer to military judgments during wartime.
items.stem: Black's opinion in Korematsu rejected which of the following arguments?
items.stimulus: Writing for the majority in Korematsu v. United States (1944), Justice Hugo Black held that Korematsu's exclusion rested not on racial hostility but on wartime military judgments about invasion fears and security, which Congress had empowered the military to act upon. — paraphrased from the majority opinion, Korematsu v. United States, 1944 (public-domain federal opinion)

option_explanations.A: Black did not reject this argument — he relied on it. His opinion accepts that Congress had empowered the military to issue the exclusion orders; congressional authorization is part of the foundation his reasoning stands on, not a claim he dismisses.
option_explanations.B: Black did not reject the sincerity of invasion fears — he took them as genuine. His opinion treats the military commanders' fears of a West Coast invasion as sincerely held judgments, which is precisely why he defers to them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Black's majority opinion insists the exclusion rested 'not on racial hostility but on wartime military judgments about invasion fears and security' — expressly rejecting the argument, pressed by Korematsu and the dissenters (notably Justice Murphy), that the policy was racial prejudice dressed up as military necessity. The opinion's central move is to reclassify a race-based order as a security measure.
option_explanations.D: Black did not reject deference to the military — he embraced it. His opinion holds that courts must defer to military judgments during wartime, which is the doctrinal basis for upholding the exclusion orders.

items.explanation: Korematsu (6–3, 1944) upheld Executive Order 9066, permitting the Army to keep over 100,000 Japanese Americans — two-thirds of them U.S. citizens — in internment camps for the rest of the war; most lost their property, and Congress apologized with $20,000 reparations in 1988.
options: (A) The military was ordered to compensate Japanese Americans for confiscated land.
(B) The military was ordered to close detention centers holding Italian and German Americans.
(C) The military was allowed to keep over 100,000 Japanese Americans interned.
(D) President Roosevelt proposed adding new justices to the Supreme Court.
items.stem: What was the most immediate consequence of the Korematsu decision?

option_explanations.A: The military was ordered to compensate no one. Korematsu upheld the internment; compensation came more than forty years later, when Congress apologized and authorized $20,000 reparations per survivor in 1988. No court in 1944 ordered payment for confiscated land.
option_explanations.B: Italian and German Americans were never mass-interned — only a small number of individuals were detained. There were no detention centers full of Italian and German Americans for the Court to order closed; the mass detention was of Japanese Americans exclusively.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Korematsu (6–3, 1944) upheld Executive Order 9066, allowing the Army to keep over 100,000 Japanese Americans — two-thirds of them U.S. citizens — in internment camps for the remainder of the war. The decision's immediate consequence was the continuation of the camps; most internees lost their property, and formal redress waited until 1988.
option_explanations.D: The court-packing plan was FDR's 1937 response to the Supreme Court striking down New Deal legislation — seven years before Korematsu and unrelated to it. Roosevelt proposed no new justices over the internment decision.
